govdocs-archive_org-MasonicTempleToPadre:
A special edition of the Italian Catholic journal Chiesa viva, number 381 of March 2006, asks whether the new church of St. Padre Pio is in fact a Masonic temple. Franco Adessa, with Father Luigi Villa, presents the case. The church at San Giovanni Rotondo, Padre Pio's town, had opened in 2004 to designs by Renzo Piano.

The authors read the building's forms, numbers, and symbols as Masonic signs hidden in a Catholic shrine. Theirs is a traditionalist polemic, richly illustrated and wholly convinced. The edition is held as it appeared: an artifact of the quarrels over modern church design and the memory of Italy's most loved modern saint.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIADowneyJohnT_:
John T. Downey was a CIA officer whose plane was shot down over China in 1952, on a mission connected with an agent extraction. Captured and sentenced to life, he spent twenty years in Chinese prisons. This Washington Post article by Thomas O'Toole, dated March 18, 1973, meets him coming home.

Downey's release came with the Nixon opening to China, and he walked out the longest-held prisoner of the CIA's early Cold War. O'Toole tells the capture, the decades in which Washington denied he was an intelligence officer, and the return. The article is the homecoming chapter of a famous spy case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarksSidTheWatl:
Sid Marks told the FBI a short story from November 23, 1963, the day after the assassination. He was in the offices of detective Dick Hathcock when Hathcock's associate, Roy Payne, came in. Payne asked whether anyone had been in to get a rifle. The bureau wrote the account up as a report, filed as LA 89-75 and known here as the Watley Report.

Reports like this one fill the assassination files by the thousand. Each preserves a single odd remark or errand that might matter. A question about a rifle, asked the day after the shooting, was exactly the kind of detail agents were told to record. The report keeps the wording, the office, and the date.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NelsonJohnT_Nel:
Harold Weisberg wrote to John T. Nelson of New Orleans on November 23, 1970. A Times-Picayune story had quoted Weisberg, and the letter takes that story as its starting point. Weisberg also describes his own independent investigations of political assassinations in New Orleans.

New Orleans was the second front of assassination research, home to the Garrison inquiry and to many Oswald leads. Weisberg worked the city by correspondence, correcting newspapers and trading findings with local contacts. The letter to Nelson shows that work at desk level: a clipping received, a reply drafted, a claim about his investigations restated for the record. It also dates his New Orleans inquiries to at least 1970.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NoguchiThomasT_: Thomas TNoguchi - the coroner to the stars - lends his name to this declassified US government file at the Internet Archive. No date, no office, no description rides along with the title. The text itself has not surfaced. A named shell, kept for completeness.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TranscriptsWash: On May 19, 1974, the Washington Post printed another White House tape transcript, the sixth in its series. Newspapers across the country raced to publish the Nixon tapes as they were released that spring. Each transcript let readers judge the president's private words for themselves. The Post's series forms a day-by-day public record of Watergate as it broke open in print.
